title: What is the DEA MATE Act 8 hour training requirement for prescribers?
description: Who must complete the DEA MATE Act one-time 8 hours of substance use disorder training, the June 27, 2023 start and the evidence, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The Medication Access and Training Expansion (MATE) Act requires every practitioner registered with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to dispense controlled substances, except practitioners who are solely veterinarians, to complete a one-time total of 8 hours of training on treating and managing patients with opioid or other substance use disorders. Practitioners attest to it by checking a box on their first DEA registration application or renewal submitted on or after June 27, 2023.
keyTakeaways: The duty was enacted by section 1263(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, signed on December 29, 2022, and is now codified at 21 U.S.C. 823(m).
It applies at the practitioner's first registration or renewal on or after June 27, 2023, which is 180 days after enactment. DEA does not ask for the attestation again at later renewals.
The 8 hours can be cumulative, can predate the law, and include past DATA waiver training, if delivered by an organization the statute lists.
Board certification in addiction medicine or addiction psychiatry, or recent graduation from a curriculum with at least 8 hours of substance use disorder content, satisfies the requirement.
DEA does not collect certificates at application, but recommends that each practitioner keep a record of training documenting completion.
regulator: Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), US Department of Justice
appliesTo: Physicians, dentists, podiatrists and other practitioners registered with DEA to dispense controlled substances in schedules II to V
Nurse practitioners and other advanced practice registered nurses, physician assistants and other non-physician practitioners holding a DEA registration under state prescriptive authority
Health systems, medical groups and credentialing teams that verify DEA registration for their prescribers
Not practitioners who are solely veterinarians

sections.heading: What does the MATE Act training requirement require?

blocks.text: It requires each qualified practitioner to complete at least 8 hours of training on the treatment and management of patients with opioid or other substance use disorders as a condition of DEA registration to dispense controlled substances in schedules II, III, IV or V. The requirement came from section 1263(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (Public Law 117-328, division FF), and is set out in the Controlled Substances Act at [21 U.S.C. 823](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/21/823). It was added as subsection (l) and redesignated subsection (m) by 2025 amendments (Public Laws 119-26 and 119-44), so older guidance cites 823(l).

A qualified practitioner is defined in 823(m)(4)(B) as a practitioner who is licensed under state law to prescribe controlled substances and is not solely a veterinarian. The statute splits practitioners into two routes: physicians under 823(m)(1)(A) and other practitioners, such as nurse practitioners and physician assistants, under 823(m)(1)(B). Each route has its own list of training providers and its own deemed groups.

blocks.title: 21 U.S.C. 823(m)(2)(A), one-time training
blocks.text: "The Attorney General shall not require any qualified practitioner to complete the training described in clause (iv) or (v) of paragraph (1)(A) or clause (i) or (ii) of paragraph (1)(B) more than once."

The topics differ slightly by route. Physicians may count training on substance use disorders or on the safe pharmacological management of dental pain combined with screening, brief intervention and referral for treatment. Non-physician practitioners count training on the treatment and management of patients with opioid or other substance use disorders. The statute allows classroom sessions, seminars at professional society meetings, electronic communications or other formats.

sections.heading: When did the requirement start, and what is the deadline?

blocks.text: The requirement started on June 27, 2023, and the deadline for each practitioner is their next DEA registration submission on or after that date, whether an initial application or a renewal. Section 823(m)(4)(A) defines the "first applicable registration" as the first registration or renewal that occurs on or after the date that is 180 days after December 29, 2022.

DEA explained the timing in its [MATE Act questions and answers](https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/faq/MATE_Act_faq.html): beginning June 27, 2023, practitioners check a box on the online registration form affirming completion, and "this one-time training requirement affirmation will not be a part of future registration renewals." DEA modified the DEA Form 224 application and the DEA Form 224a renewal to carry the attestation.

Under [21 CFR 1301.13(d)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/1301.13), a practitioner registration expires 36 months after its initial expiration date. As a result, most practitioners already registered before June 27, 2023 will have met their first applicable registration by mid 2026, and as at November 2026 the requirement bites mainly on new applicants and on anyone whose registration lapsed. Organizations should still confirm each prescriber's attestation rather than assume it.

sections.heading: Who is treated as already meeting the training requirement?

blocks.text: Two groups are deemed to have satisfied the training without separate coursework. The [DEA letter to registrants dated March 27, 2023](https://www.deadiversion.usdoj.gov/pubs/docs/MATE_Training_Letter_Final.pdf), issued under the statute's 90 day notification duty, describes them as follows.

items: **Group 1:** practitioners board certified in addiction medicine or addiction psychiatry by the American Board of Medical Specialties, the American Board of Addiction Medicine or the American Osteopathic Association.

**Group 2:** practitioners who graduated in good standing from a US medical (allopathic or osteopathic), dental, physician assistant or advanced practice nursing school within five years of June 27, 2023, and completed a comprehensive curriculum that included at least 8 hours of training on treating substance use disorders, including the clinical use of all drugs approved by the Food and Drug Administration for that purpose, or on safe pharmacological management of dental pain with screening, brief intervention and referral.

blocks.text: The statute words the graduation route as graduation during the 5 year period immediately preceding the date the practitioner first registers or renews, so the curriculum must be documented, not assumed. Everyone else meets the requirement by completing 8 hours of qualifying training from a listed provider.

sections.heading: What training counts toward the 8 hours?

blocks.text: Any 8 hours on the treatment and management of patients with opioid or other substance use disorders counts if a provider named in the statute delivered it. DEA's letter sets out four rules that matter for training records:

items: The training does not have to occur in one session and can be cumulative across multiple sessions.
Past training counts, including training received before the law was enacted on December 29, 2022.
Past DATA waiver training, the course formerly needed to prescribe buprenorphine for opioid use disorder, counts toward the 8 hours.
Classroom settings, seminars at professional society meetings and virtual offerings are all acceptable.

blocks.text: The DEA letter lists the providers for the physician route, including the American Society of Addiction Medicine, the American Academy of Addiction Psychiatry, the American Medical Association, the American Osteopathic Association, the American Dental Association, the American Psychiatric Association, the American Association of Nurse Practitioners, the American Academy of Physician Associates and the American Nurses Credentialing Center, plus any organization accredited by the Accreditation Council for Continuing Medical Education (ACCME) or the Commission for Continuing Education Provider Recognition. The current statutory text for non-physician practitioners also names the American Pharmacists Association, the Accreditation Council for Pharmacy Education, the American Psychiatric Nurses Association, the American Academy of Nursing and the American Academy of Family Physicians.

sections.heading: What evidence should practitioners and employers keep?

blocks.text: Practitioners should keep certificates or other documents showing completion, because DEA relies on a self-attestation. DEA's question and answer guidance states that it "is recommended that each practitioner keep a record of training certificates or other materials documenting completion," and that these documents "will not need to be submitted to DEA for review at the time of initial application or renewal of registration."

Because the attestation is a statement on a federal registration application, a credentialing file that holds the certificates, the provider's accreditation and the hours makes the attestation defensible. The same records support privileging decisions and payer credentialing. For retention periods across other obligations, see [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does the MATE Act interact with state opioid training rules?

blocks.text: It sits alongside them. Section 823(m)(3) says nothing in the subsection precludes using the training to satisfy a state registration requirement, and nothing preempts additional state requirements on dispensing controlled substances. Many state boards run their own recurring opioid or controlled substance courses.

The New York State Department of Health, for example, states on its [mandatory prescriber education page](https://www.health.ny.gov/professionals/narcotic/mandatory_prescriber_education/) that its 3 hours of training in pain management, palliative care and addiction every three years is in addition to the federal 8 hour training. State medical boards such as those in Florida, Pennsylvania and Texas also set recurring opioid content, compared in [physician CME requirements by state](/regulations/physician-cme-requirements-by-state).

sections.heading: How can a health system map the MATE Act to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: A short obligation map lets a medical staff office track the one-time duty next to recurring state rules, using the same approach as a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix). The table below is an original summary built from the statute and DEA guidance.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records the MATE Act as a one-time obligation tied to an event, the first applicable DEA registration, rather than to a calendar cycle, and links it to the state obligations that can share the same training hours. Each prescriber's evidence points back to the statutory clause it satisfies, so a credentialing reviewer can see why a certificate counts. More detail is on the [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) page.

faqs.q: Do I have to repeat the MATE Act training at every DEA renewal?
faqs.a: No. The statute bars DEA from requiring the training more than once, and DEA's guidance says the attestation will not be part of future registration renewals. Once a practitioner has attested at their first registration or renewal on or after June 27, 2023, the federal duty is complete, although state rules may require separate recurring opioid education.

faqs.q: Does the MATE Act apply to pharmacists?
faqs.a: It applies to practitioners who hold a DEA registration to dispense controlled substances under state prescriptive authority and are not solely veterinarians. A pharmacist who holds such a practitioner registration under state law would fall within the definition. Pharmacists who dispense only under a pharmacy registration are not practitioner registrants and are not the target of the attestation.

faqs.q: Can a 12 hour state pain management course count toward the 8 hours?
faqs.a: Hours count if the content covers the treatment and management of patients with opioid or other substance use disorders and the provider is one the statute lists, such as an ACCME accredited organization. Hours on unrelated pain topics may not qualify. The statute expressly allows the same training to be used for state requirements as well.

faqs.q: What happens if a practitioner checks the box without completing the training?
faqs.a: The attestation is a statement made on a federal registration application. DEA guidance recommends keeping completion records because DEA may ask for them. Organizations should treat an unsupported attestation as a credentialing risk and confirm documentation before relying on it.
